So, if you're born on or before 27 June 1960, you might get a Winter Fuel Payment (WFP) of £100 to £300 for the 2026-2027 winter. This is auto for most who qualify, and you'll hear in Oct/Nov how much you're getting (letter). Payback is from HMRC if your income > £35k, no worry 'bout your partner's income though. ✅Scotland exception: no WFP, check Pension Age Winter Heating payment instead. 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮�长城: Yeah, you're good here for WFP, if you live in England/Wales/Northern Ireland.

Watch out for scams - legit msgs won't ask for bank details or passwords. Report anything dodgy. Other heating help: Cold Weather Pay if temps hit 0°C for 7 days straight, Warm Home Discount ($150 off your bill) if Pension Credit or low-income, local council help if you qualify. 📋

Not eligible if:
- Live outside Eng/Wales/N Ireland
- Visiting Eng/Wales/N Ireland 21-27 Sep 2026
- In hospital all that week and the year before
- Need permission to enter UK and can't claim public funds
- In prison all that week

Care home dweller? You can still get WFP unless you get Universal Credit, Pension Credit, or income-related ESA and have been in the care home since 29 June 2026. 🏡

If no letter by Nov and you think you should qualify, check if you need to claim. Money based on when born & circumstances 21-27 Sep 2026. No impact on other benefits.

Income > £35k, HMRC takes it back via tax code or Self Assessment. Check income threshold and how HMRC will take it.

Living alone or with someone not eligible:
- £200 if born 28 Sep 1946 to 27 Jun 1960
- £300 if born before 28 Sep 1946

Living with someone eligible? Different rates apply. 📝

P.S. Guide in Welsh (Cymraeg) & easy read version available. 📜

Pension Credit = extra cash if u're over State Pension age & low on cash. It's a thing for housing costs too like ground rent & service charges. FYI, this guide is in Welsh (Cymraeg) & easy read if u prefer. 🇪🇦

Got a carer, severely disabled or looking after a kid? You might get extra help. Pension Credit ≠ State Pension (it's a whole 'nother thing). Even if u have other income, savings or own a house, u can still apply for it. 🏡

This only covers Eng, Sct & Wal. Nort'n Ireland's different, check separately. 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿

If u get Pension Credit, u might also get: Housing Benefit if renting Cold Weather Payments (or Winter Heating in Scotland) Support for Mortgage Interest if u own yer place Council Tax Reduction free TV licence if yer 75+ NHS stuff: glasses, dental, transport for hospital visits (if u get Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit) help with heating through Warm Home Discount Scheme postal discount when moving house 🏃‍♂️

To get Pension Credit, u must live in Eng, Sct or Wal & be at State Pension age. Nort'n Ireland's different. 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁮󠁿

From the EU/Switzerland/Norway/Iceland/Liechtenstein? U & ur fam need settled or pre-settled status under EU Settlement Scheme (deadline was June 30, 2021, but check if u can still apply).

If u have a partner, gotta include them on the app. You're eligible if: Both of u are at State Pension age or one of u is getting Housing Benefit for over State Pension age. 🧑‍🤝‍🧑

Partner = husband, wife, civil partner or someone u live with as a couple. 🤷‍♂️

Income Calc: When u apply, they'll look at ur income. If u have a partner, they'll calc together. The top-ups are: £238 if single & £363.25 if u have a partner. Higher income? Still might be eligible if u have a disability, care for someone, have savings or housing costs.

What counts as income: State Pension other pens earnings from job or self-emp most social security benefits (e.g., Carer’s Allowance)

What doesn't count as income: Adult Disability Payment Attendance Allowance Child Benefit Christmas Bonus Council Tax Reduction Disability Living Allowance Housing Benefit Pension Age Disability Payment Personal Independence Payment Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance social fund payments like Winter Fuel Payment

If u deferred yer pension: Personal or workplace pension not claimed yet? Expected amount still counts as income. If u deferred yer State Pension, the amt u'd get still counts. 🙃

So yea, just a quick rundown. Hope this helps! 🍀

So, hey there! If you’re thinking about finance for uni or college, you could look into student finance. You can apply for a Tuition Fee Loan to help with the uni fees and a Maintenance Loan to cover rent, food, books, travel—basically, living costs. The Tuition Fee Loan goes straight to your uni and the Maintenance Loan hits your bank acct. Got to pay it back, but only once you finish or leave and earn a certain amount. No sweat right now. 😅

If you're low-income, disabled, or have kids, you might get extra help that you don’t usually pay back. Even if you’re not from the UK, you might still be able to apply. Check eligibility real quick. Oh, and if your course starts after Jan 1, 2027, the rules are changin'. 🔄 Log in if you're a returning student or already have an account.

Before you apply, note that your monthly repayment depends on your earnings, not how much you owe. You get interest from day 1, and these loans don’t show up on credit reports. But mortgage lenders might count it. Terms and conditions can change, so read Student loans: a guide to terms and conditions for 2025-2026 and 2026-2027. Also, check the privacy notice. If you need help, you can let someone else apply for you, like your mum or dad using Power of Attorney.

How to apply? Check the guide. If you're under 25 with no contact with your parents, you can apply as an ‘estranged student’ through UCAS. If you were in care before turning 16 for 13+ weeks, you can apply through UCAS as a care leaver. 

If you’re not from England, it gets a bit more complex. Got different rules for Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, Jersey, Guernsey, and Isle of Man. You can still get the Tuition Fee Loan, Maintenance Loan, and extra funding.

If your course starts after Jan 1, 2027, check what’s new. What you qualify for depends on your uni, your course, past higher ed, age, and residency status. Contact your uni or college to confirm if your course is eligible. For full-time studies, it’s gotta be a qualifying course like a BA, BSc, BEd, foundation degree, CertHE, DipHE, HNC, HND, etc. 

Got all that? 🤔 Hope it helps!

Okay, so here’s the lowdown on Jobcentre Plus stuff:

- You can hit up Jobcentre Plus for new ben claims, existing ones, and appt changes. 📝
- If you need it in Cymraeg, it’s available. 👍
- Find your local Jobcentre details via the local office search. Just use the address from there to write if you need to. Usually, it's on the letters you’ve got. 📫

For Northern Ireland, remember:
- JSA? Go to Jobs and Benefits office. 
- ESA? ESA Centre. 🇬🇧

Complaining? Yeah, you can do that. 😒

Want a job? Use the ‘Find a job’ service. 🆕

Need a National Insurance number? Apply or find it if lost. 👤

Employers: Advertise a job or get recruitment help from Jobcentre Plus.

For claiming New Style JSA, apply online unless under 18 or applying for someone else. Can’t apply online? Call 0800 055 6688. For BSL, use 18001 then 0800 055 6688 or the video relay service. Welsh? 0800 012 1888. Mon-Fri, 8am-5pm.

Different contact details? Call for:
- Universal Credit
- New Style ESA
- Alternative formats (braille, large print, audio CD). 😖

Benefits calc? Use it to find your benefits eligibility. When calling, you’ll need your NI number. For JSA, Incapacity, ESA:
- 0800 169 0310 (Relay UK: 18001 then 0800 169 0310)
- BSL: use the video relay service.
- Welsh: 0800 169 0207. Mon-Fri, 8am-5pm.

Northern Ireland JSA? Jobs and Benefits office. ESA? ESA Centre. 🚪

Universal Credit? Sign in to your online account or call the helpline. Mon-Fri, 8am-6pm.

Social Fund? 0800 169 0140 (Relay UK: 18001 then 0800 169 A140, BSL: video relay). Mon-Fri, 10am-3pm. Welsh: 0800 169 0240. Mon-Fri, 8am-5pm. 📞

And that’s the gist! Call charges apply, so check 'em. 📢

So, the benefit cap is basically a max amount of money in benefits one can get. It’s mainly for folks over 16 but not at State Pension age yet. The guide is in Welsh (Cymraeg) too if anyone needs that 🇦🇼.

The cap affects these benefits:
- UC (Universal Credit)
- Bereavement Allowance
- Child Benefit
- ESA (Employment and Support Allowance)
- HB (Housing Benefit)
- Incapacity Benefit
- JSA (Jobseeker’s Allowance)
- Maternity Allowance
- SD (Severe Disablement Allowance)
- Widowed Parent’s Allowance (or Widowed Mother’s Allowance or Widow’s Pension)

If you’re over State Pension age, you’re good. And if you're a couple, it might not apply if one is over State Pension age. But if you or your partner gets UC for a disability or health issue that stops you from working (they call it ‘limited capability for work and work-related activity’), or you care for someone with a disability, you’re cool.

Also, if you and your partner earn £881+ a month together, you're not affected. And if you or your partner or kids under 18 get any of these:
- ADP (Adult Disability Payment)
- Armed Forces Comp. Scheme
- Armed Forces Indep. Payment
- Attendance Allowance
- Carer’s Allowance
- Carer Support Payment
- Child Disability Payment
- DLA (Disability Living Allowance)
- ESA support component
- Guardian’s Allowance
- Industrial Injuries Benefits
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- PIP (Personal Independence Payment)
- SADLA (Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance)
- War pensions
- War Widow’s or War Widower’s Pension,

you’re not affected either. 📝

For UC claimants, the cap might not start for 9 months, depending on your earnings. This is called the 'grace period'. To get it, you have to meet these:
- You stopped working or your earnings went down
- Now earning less than £881/mo
- For the 12 months before, you earned the same or more than the threshold (it was £846 til March 31, 2026, then £881 from April 1, 2026).

Report your earnings from the past 12 months when applying for UC. And if separated from your partner, their earnings still count for the time you lived together.

That's the gist of it. Hope this helps! 📑

So, hey there! Welcome! 😅 Here's what you need to know about the whole terrorism thing going on in the UK. 

- **Threat Level**: It’s super serious. For the UK as a whole, it's **severe** (that means an attack is highly likely). For Northern Ireland, it's **substantial** (so, likely but not as bad). There are 5 levels total: low, moderate, substantial, severe, and critical. Got it?

- **Who’s in Charge**: The Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre and MI5 (that’s the Security Service) decide the threat level. They can change it anytime, no warning or expiration date. 🔔

- **More Info**: Check the MI5 website for all the details, and the government’s travel advice for other countries. 👍

- **Roles**: MI5 protects the UK, and the Office for Security and Counter-Terrorism handles the big stuff if something happens. The cops enforce the laws. 🚔

- **Public Safety**: The government might give a warning if there's a specific threat. If you see or think something’s off:
  - Call the police or report online.
  - Report suspicious activity to MI5.
  - You can stay anonymous, FYI. 🙃

- **National Risk Register**: The government keeps a list of hazards and threats, and the National Risk Register tells you how likely they are and what might happen. 📑

- **Preparations**: Your local council, fire, police, and ambulance folks do regular training. Check out what’s happening in your area. 🧑‍🚒

- **Recovery**: There's guidance for local councils on how to recover after an emergency. Plus, the government has plans to keep essential services running. 🏥🏥

Hope that helps! 🤞

Hey, so Council Tax bands are based on stupid old valuations: 1991 for England, 2003 for Wales. Crazy, right? They even have a Welsh version of this guide (Cymraeg).

If you think your band is wrong, you can challenge it. There’s a legal way (‘making a proposal’) and a not-so-legal way (‘band review’). For England and Wales, hit up the Valuation Office. In Scotland, go to your local Valuation Joint Board or council. Find them on the Scottish Assessors Association site.

You can 'make a proposal' if you’ve been paying for less than 6 months or the Valuation Office (VO) changed your band recently. Also if:

- Your property changed (split or merged)
- Use changed (part for business now)
- Local area changed (new supermarket or road)

To remove a property from the list (so you don’t pay tax):

- Demolished
- Derelict or seriously broken (like a collapsed ceiling)
- Major renovations (all/most of the property)
- Now a business, no longer domestic

You can’t just say it’s ‘poor repair’. More details here on what actually counts as derelict.

Once removed, you stop paying until it’s fixed or becomes domestic again. Then reassessed, start paying from completion or move-in date.

To add a property to the list, it just needs to not have a band yet. Suggest a band.

Info you need to provide:

- Your name
- Property address
- Date for proposal
- Homeowner or tenant

For property or area changes, also need:

- Description of changes
- Details of use change
- How local area changed
- Physical works details

Hope this helps, it’s a mess. Cheers!

OK, so APT stands for Assured Periodic Tenancy. Super important. If you’re doing anything else, like regulated tenancies, forget this and look elsewhere. For it to be an APT, you gotta tick these boxes:  

- You don’t live there.
- It’s their main home.
- They have their own room (bathrooms and kitchens can be shared - no biggie).

Things that automatically disqualify it from being an APT:
- You live there part-time (or full-time).
- It’s student accommodation under the National Code.
- Fixed term over 21 years (seriously, who does that?).
- Rent is super high or super low.
- Business or licensed premises.
- Holiday let.

**Key point:** No more ASTs (Assured Shorthold Tenancies). They all became APTs on 1 May 2026. 

### Tenancy Agreement:
- Yep, you need one. It’s a contract with terms for renting the place out.
- Can be written or just a verbal agreement. But if it’s verbal, write down the key stuff and give it to the tenant.
- Joint tenancy if more than one tenant signs the same agreement. They’re all on the hook for the rent.

### Tenancy Duration:
- You can’t set a fixed end date. If you do, it’s a no-go and you could get fined.
- Must be rolling, like weekly or monthly, no longer than a month at a time.
- Ends when:
  - You both agree to end it.
  - Tenant decides to end it.
  - You regain possession.

### Rent and Advertising:
- Rent bidding is a no-no. If someone offers more than the advertised rent, tell them no and beware of a £7,000 fine.
- When you advertise:
  - Must specify the rent amount.
  - Cannot use a price range.
  - Applies to any written ad: online, print, social media, emails, texts.

That’s it! Got any questions, just shout.

If you get discriminated against, you can:

- Complain directly.

Blind Person’s Allowance (BPA) = extra tax-free moolah. Adds to your yearly Personal Allowance. So you earn more before tax kicks in. FYI, for 2026-2027, BPA is £3,250, and 2025-2026, it's £3,130. If you and your spouse/civil partner both can get it, you each get an allowance. You can transfer your BPA to them if you don't pay tax or don't earn enough to use it all. For prev. years, check the Income Tax rates & allowances guidance.

For England & Wales:
- Need to be registered as blind/severely sight impaired with local council.
- Must have a certificate saying you’re blind/severely sight impaired or similar doc from a doc.

For Scotland & NI:
- Just need to prove you can't do work that needs eyesight.

To claim, contact HMRC:
- 0300 200 3301
- Mon-Fri, 8am-6pm (no bank holidays)

Transfer allowance to spouse/civil partner if:
- Married or in a civil partnership
- Living with them (or unable to due to illness, work, prison, training, etc.)

To transfer, use form 575 or call HMRC. Also, you might get the option to transfer Married Couple’s Allowance. If filing form R40 for tax back on savings, tick the box to get form 575.

If you need form 575 in different format (like Braille), hit up HMRC.

Corp Tax rate = 25% for most. If you're over £250k profit, it's the main rate. Under £50k profit, you're at 19%. 🤓 Between £50k and £250k, you might get Marginal Relief. Thresholds get shrunk for short periods or if you've got associated companies. Oil folks, you've got special rates. 🤢

Old rates: Single rate from 1 Apr 2015 to 31 Mar 2023. Before 1 Apr 2015, rates depended on profit size. Figure out your profits on the Tax Return.

Deductions? Yeah, you can deduct some biz costs. Got to figure if it's a capital or revenue expense. Only revenue can be deducted (unless it's a no-no, like entertaining). Capital expenses = long-term stuff, like buying a van or land for a warehouse. Can't deduct these from Corp Tax but might get capital allowances. Revenue expenses = daily biz costs, like trading stock or property development stuff. 🏢

Keep super detailed records and talk to an accountant if you're confused. Make sure you understand each expense and its purpose. 📒

- High num = harder qual (duh)
- Need to know a qual's level?

  - Use that Register of Regulated Quals if you know the name & exam board

- Scotland: Skills Development Scotland

There are 9 levels, okay? 9. And here they are in a super random order:

- Entry level: 3 sub-levels (1, 2, 3). Entry 3 is the hardest.
  - You got entry level awards, ELCs, diplomas, ESOL (for non-native speakers), essential skills, and functional skills

So, if you got a problem with your neighbour, here's what you do:

1. First, try talking to them. Informal chat. Like, "Hey, the dog's barking is keeping me up." Keep it chill. If they're a tenant, maybe talk to the landlord. Sometimes they listen!
   - PS: If you prefer, write a letter. Just stick to the facts. **No emotions!**

2. If that doesn’t work, consider a mediation service. Like a middleman who helps you and your neighbour agree on something. Usually faster and cheaper than court.
   - How to find one? Depends on where you live:
     - England/Wales: Civil Mediation Council
     - Scotland: Scottish Mediation Network
     - Your council or housing association might help too.

3. If the issue is a statutory nuisance (like loud music or barking dogs), hit up your local council. **But only if talking didn’t work.**
   - Statutory nuisances can be:
     - Loud music / barking dogs
     - Artificial light (not street lamps)
     - Dust/smoke/fumes from businesses
     - Build-up of rubbish
   - The council has to investigate, but it's a last resort after talking/mediation.

4. If someone’s being violent or harassing you, contact the police. That’s not a neighbour dispute; that’s a safety issue.

5. If all else fails, you can take legal action through the courts. But really, try everything else first.

6. Citizens Advice is good for practical advice on common disputes. Check ‘em out.

7. If it's a hedge issue (like, it's too tall, and it's messing with your property enjoyment):
   - Again, try talking first. Then, if no luck, ask your council for a complaint form. But it might cost you.

8. And remember, you can trim tree branches or roots that cross into your property, but only up to the property line. Don’t go overboard!

Hope that helps. Good luck! 🍀

Hey there, so if you're thinking about representing yourself in court cuz you can't afford a lawyer or you think you can speak better for yourself, here's the lowdown:

- You can get legal aid if you're in a civil (non-criminal) case and can't afford legal fees. Worth checking.
- The guide is also in Welsh (Cymraeg) if that's your thing.
- Read Advicenow’s guides for advice on how to handle your case. Scotland's different tho, so ymmv.

Someone with you in court:
- Can bring a 'McKenzie friend' to take notes and give advice, but they can't speak for you or sign docs. The judge decides if this is cool.
- Check out the McKenzie friend guidance.

Communication help:
- If you need help understanding or taking part in your hearing, ask for an intermediary. They can rephrase questions and make sure you get what's happening.
- Request an intermediary by email, post, or in person.

Legal advice:
- Still can get legal advice even if you're rep'ing yourself. Find a solicitor, or check out advice on prepping for court for debt, disputes, or personal injury.

Terms:
- If you brought the case, you're the 'applicant' (e.g., filed divorce papers).
- If you're responding to divorce papers or a separation request, you're the 'respondent'.

Before court:
- Mediation is usually a must before you go to court. No C100 form sent, no court hearing.
- Read up on when to take your case to court and what happens with a 'Guide for Separated Parents: Children and the Family Courts'.
- Also find out how to apply for a court order, types of orders, and what happens after you apply.

Pretrial prep:
- Mediation is a must, and don’t forget the C100 form.
- Can still get legal advice even if you're doing it solo.
- Read about what to expect at court.

Evidence and witnesses:
- Bring docs as evidence and show 'em to the judge and prosecution on trial day.
- Bring copies if you can.

Court day:
- Read Advicenow’s guide for when the other side has a lawyer and you don’t.

Hope this helps!

Hey new guy/gal! Here are some quick notes on the Adult Dependants’ Grant (ADG). It's kinda important if someone's relying on you financially and you're in school:

- If you're in full-time higher ed or doin' 120+ credits funded by the LLE, you might qualify for up to £3,545.
- This money is extra on top of your other student finance and you don't have to pay it back, BUT if your situation changes and you get overpaid, you might have to give some back.
- If you’re gettin' a Postgrad Loan, forget about the ADG.
- The ADG affects income-related benefits you might get. So, watch out for that!
- How much you get depends on your income, the adult dependant’s income, and your personal stuff (e.g., if you’re married or have kids).
- You’ll get paid in up to 3 installments a year, straight into your bank account.

For the ADG, another adult has to depend on you financially and they can’t be:
- Your kid
- A relative who makes over £3,796 a year
- Getting student finance
- Your partner if you’re under 25 - unless you're married or in a civil partnership.

You’re also out of luck if:
- Your household income is over £15,835.98.
- You’re gettin' a Postgrad Loan.

Remember, if your course starts on or after 1 Aug 2026, the adult who depends on you must live in the UK, or they’ll get less if they live there part-time. 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿

On your main student finance app, fill in the ADG section and give some estimates on your household income. Student Finance England (SFE) will check it out and might ask for:
- Your P60
- Child Benefit details
- Partner's financial info like bank statements

If an adult who depends on you starts claiming student finance and you’re already gettin' the ADG, let SFE know ASAP!

- Unlimited fine or jail for up to 6 months.

- Intentionally using your dog to hurt someone? You could get charged with 'malicious wounding'.
- If your dog kills someone, it’s 14 years or a huge fine.
- Harming an assistance dog? 3 years or a fine.

If you have a banned dog, the police or council dog warden can take it away. No warrant needed if in public, but they need one if in a private place. If the dog expert says it’s banned, it can be kept or destroyed.

From Nov 1, 2026, no leaving a kid under 12 alone with a banned dog in a private place without an adult around.

XL Bullies: You gotta have a Certificate of Exemption to own one. Check the rules for your area.

Got all that? It’s a lot, but just remember, keep your dog in check or you’re looking at some serious trouble.

So yea, there's 14 allergens businesses gotta tell you about. Big deal, right?

Restaurants:
- They gotta give you info on allergens, like if it’s in the food or not.
- Check online menus if they have one 'cause it's a thing.
- Call ahead & ask:
  - If they have meals that work for you
  - How they handle food in the kitchen
  - If there's a chance of cross-contamination
- When you go there, you can remind them & ask again. Also, if they changed any ingredients & if they can cook something different for you, but they don't have to, FYI.

Takeaways:
- Must tell you if the food has any of the 14 allergens.
- They gotta do this in writing on the website/menu or by phone before you buy.
- Also when the food is delivered, either with stickers on the container or in person by the delivery guy.
- If ordering for a group, you can ask them to label the containers so you know which one's yours.

PPDS (Prepacked for Direct Sale) food:
- This is like boxed sandwiches or wrapped burgers. They should be labeled with the food name & ingredients, with the 14 allergens highlighted.

Allergens they gotta mention:
celery, gluten cereals (wheat, rye, barley, oats), crustaceans (prawns, crabs, lobsters), eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs (mussels, oysters), mustard, nuts (almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, brazil nuts, cashews, pecans, pistachios, macadamia nuts), peanuts, sesame, soybeans, sulfur dioxide/sulfites (more than 10ppm)

If allergic to something else, just ask!

Important: If you feel sick or have an allergic reaction, get medical help immediately. NHS has info on allergic reactions & how to treat them. Carry your adrenaline auto-injector (AAI) & use it if you think you're having a reaction.

Reporting an allergic reaction:
- Contact the business that sold you the food & tell them.
- You can also report it to your local council’s food safety team.

Support & Alerts:
- There are orgs like Allergy UK, Coeliac UK, Anaphylaxis UK, Natasha Allergy Research Foundation that can help.
- You can sign up for free alerts for missing/incorrect allergy info by email or text. Choose to get alerts for all allergens or just your allergy. Just sign up to aller...

P.S. The guide is also in Welsh (Cymraeg).
